fuentes/etiquetas-de-la-tumba-u-j/titulo.texto: Tags and vessels with signs from Tomb U-j at Abydos

fuentes/etiquetas-de-la-tumba-u-j/autor.texto: Scribes of the ruler buried in Tomb U-j

fuentes/etiquetas-de-la-tumba-u-j/soport.texto: Bone and ivory tags and marks on vessels

fuentes/etiquetas-de-la-tumba-u-j/resume.texto: Some 186 perforated bone and ivory tags, with proto-hieroglyphic signs, found in Tomb U-j of the U cemetery at Umm el-Qaab, dated to Naqada IIIA2. Its excavator, Günter Dreyer, read them as indications of the origin of goods. Other researchers interpret the signs as place names or divine names.

fuentes/etiquetas-de-la-tumba-u-j/por_qu.texto: They are cited as the earliest evidence of writing in Egypt and as a sign of a developed administration already in place before the First Dynasty.

fuentes/cabeza-de-maza-de-escorpion/auto.texto: Scribes and craftsmen of King Scorpion

fuentes/cabeza-de-maza-de-escorpion/resu.texto: Limestone macehead found in the main deposit of the Horus temple at Hierakonpolis by Quibell and Green in 1897-1898. A scorpion carved beside the figure of the king wearing the white crown led to its attribution to a king named Scorpion (c. 3200-3000 BC).

fuentes/cabeza-de-maza-de-escorpion/por_.texto: It is one of the documents with which the ritual and kingship of Upper Egypt just before the First Dynasty are studied.

fuentes/cabeza-de-maza-de-narmer/resumen.texto: Limestone macehead about 20 cm high, found by James Quibell in 1898 in the main deposit of the temple of Nekhen (Hierakonpolis), with the serekh of Narmer carved on it. It is dated to the reign of Narmer and is now in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford.

fuentes/cabeza-de-maza-de-narmer/por_que.texto: Together with the Narmer Palette, it is one of the objects from the Hierakonpolis deposit with which kingship at the beginning of Egyptian history is studied.

fuentes/paleta-del-campo-de-batalla/sopo.texto: Carved stone cosmetic palette, in two pieces

fuentes/paleta-del-campo-de-batalla/resu.texto: Cosmetic palette of the Naqada III phase, perhaps from Abydos, whose two main pieces are in the British Museum and the Ashmolean. It may be the earliest battle scene on an Egyptian ornamental palette, and it includes standards and a prisoner that are precursors of hieroglyphs.

fuentes/paleta-del-campo-de-batalla/por_.texto: It is used to study how war was depicted and how the first hieroglyphic signs appear before the First Dynasty.

fuentes/paleta-del-toro/soporte.texto: Fragment of a greywacke cosmetic palette with relief

fuentes/paleta-del-toro/resumen.texto: Fragment of a greywacke cosmetic palette from Naqada III, now in the Louvre. On the obverse there is a large fortified town and, on the reverse, figures that later became hieroglyphs, such as the closed fist, standards with animals, the ibis, the falcon of Horus, and the lightning bolt of the Min symbol.

fuentes/paleta-del-toro/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the iconographic documents of the preparation of Egyptian kingship just before the First Dynasty.

fuentes/paleta-libia/soporte.texto: Lower part of a carved schist cosmetic palette

fuentes/paleta-libia/resumen.texto: Lower part of a schist cosmetic palette, 19 cm long, found at Abydos and dated to Naqada III or the Protodynastic period. It is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and is also called the Libyan Booty Palette or the Tehenu Palette.

fuentes/paleta-libia/por_que_importa.texto: It is cited in studies of the earliest images of war and of fortified towns in Egypt.

fuentes/paleta-de-los-cazadores/soporte.texto: Cosmetic palette with relief, in two fragments

fuentes/paleta-de-los-cazadores/resumen.texto: Cosmetic palette from Naqada III, around 3100 BC, with a lion-hunt scene. It is broken: one part is in the British Museum and another in the Louvre. It was registered as found in the El-Amarna area, probably through a confusion, and Budge later said it came from Abydos.

fuentes/paleta-de-los-cazadores/por_que_.texto: It is another of the iconographic documents with which hunting and kingship before the First Dynasty are studied.

fuentes/paleta-de-oxford/resumen.texto: Cosmetic palette, also called the Two Dogs Palette, discovered by Quibell and Green in the main deposit of the Horus temple at Hierakonpolis during the 1897-1898 campaign. It belongs to the collection of the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford.

fuentes/paleta-de-oxford/por_que_importa.texto: It belongs to the same group of Hierakonpolis objects as the Narmer Palette and the Scorpion Macehead.

fuentes/lista-real-de-saqqara/autor.texto: Scribes of the time of Ramesses II

fuentes/lista-real-de-saqqara/soporte.texto: Relief from the tomb of the scribe Tjuneroy

fuentes/lista-real-de-saqqara/resumen.texto: List of royal cartouches found in a tomb at Saqqara, from the time of Ramesses II: 58 kings, from Anedjib to Ramesses II, in reverse order. It includes Neferkasokar, Hudjefa, and Huni, who are missing from the Abydos King List, and it omits everything from Pepi II to Mentuhotep II.

fuentes/lista-real-de-saqqara/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the three Ramesside royal lists used to check the successions of the Old Kingdom.

fuentes/south-saqqara-stone/resumen.texto: Lid of the sarcophagus of Queen Ankhesenpepi IV, inscribed with a list of the reigns of the kings of the Sixth Dynasty, from Teti, Userkare, Pepi I, and Merenre to the first years of Pepi II, under whom it was probably made. It is an annalistic document that records the events of each year of a reign; about 92 % of the original text was lost when the stone was polished for reuse as a lid.

fuentes/south-saqqara-stone/por_que_impo.texto: It is the closest surviving annalistic document of the Sixth Dynasty to its own time, although it is heavily damaged.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-weni/resumen.texto: Text carved in the funerary chapel of Weni the Elder at Abydos, an official of the Sixth Dynasty; a second tomb of his in the necropolis of Pepi I at Saqqara has an almost identical copy. It narrates his career under Teti, Pepi I, and Merenre, the investigation of a conspiracy in the royal harem, the campaign against the peoples of the east, and expeditions to extract stone.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-weni/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the main sources on the army and administration under Pepi I, and it survives in two tombs.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-weni/leer.0.tit.texto: Translation by J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. I (1906), on Internet Archive

fuentes/autobiografia-de-harkhuf/resumen.texto: Inscription in the tomb of Harkhuf at Qubbet el-Hawa. It describes his journeys to Yam, in Nubia: three under Merenre and a fourth in year 2 of Pepi II. It also reproduces a letter from the young Pepi II about a dwarf that Harkhuf was bringing.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-harkhuf/por_que.texto: It is one of the two most important and famous autobiographies of Old Kingdom officials, and the main source on contacts with Nubia.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-harkhuf/leer.0..texto: Translation by J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. I (1906), on Internet Archive

fuentes/inscripcion-de-metjen/titulo.texto: Inscription from the Tomb of Metjen

fuentes/inscripcion-de-metjen/resumen.texto: Biographical text from the tomb of Metjen, a senior official at the transition from the Third to the Fourth Dynasty, who claims to have served under Huni and Snefru.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-metjen/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the oldest tomb biographies and gives information on land allotments and administration in the early Fourth Dynasty.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-metjen/leer.0.tit.texto: Translation by J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. I (1906), on Internet Archive

fuentes/instrucciones-de-kagemni/resumen.texto: Wisdom text (sebayt) preserved in the Prisse Papyrus, where the end of an instruction addressed to a Kagemni appears. Tradition attributed it to the vizier Kagemni, who served Snefru according to that same tradition, although the author of the text has no name. The earliest proof of its composition dates from the Middle Kingdom.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-kagemni/por_que.texto: It illustrates how the Middle Kingdom represented the court of the Old Kingdom, and it should be read as a later work.

fuentes/instrucciones-de-kagemni/leer.0..texto: Translation by B. Gunn, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep and the Instruction of Ke'gemni (Wisdom of the East, 1912 ed.), on Internet Archive

fuentes/instruccion-para-merikare/resume.texto: Literary text in Middle Egyptian, probably from the Middle Kingdom (2055-1650 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), in which a king of the First Intermediate Period, perhaps named Kheti, advises his son, the future king Merikare. It alludes to the war with the South, which would be the Eleventh Dynasty of Thebes.

fuentes/instruccion-para-merikare/por_qu.texto: It is the main literary source on the kings of Herakleopolis, although its date of composition and its accuracy are debated.

fuentes/instruccion-de-hordjedef/soporte.texto: New Kingdom ostraca and a late-period wooden tablet

fuentes/instruccion-de-hordjedef/resumen.texto: Wisdom text (sebayt) whose opening names as its author the prince Djedefhor, son of Khufu. According to Miriam Lichtheim it is possibly the oldest of the known teachings, composed in the Fifth Dynasty; only fragments of the beginning survive, on a few New Kingdom ostraca and a late-period wooden tablet.

fuentes/instruccion-de-hordjedef/por_que.texto: It shows the reputation as a sage that Djedefhor had in later tradition, which names him alongside Imhotep.

fuentes/rey-neferkare-y-el-general-sasen.texto: Fragmentary papyri and ostraca from the late New Kingdom

Tale surviving only in fragments, in three sources from the late New Kingdom, though it was composed earlier. It purports to describe the nighttime outings of Pepi II Neferkare; the story censures the king's conduct, and it is often cited in debates about homosexuality in ancient Egypt.
It is a later literary tradition about Pepi II, not a testimony of his reign.

fuentes/diario-de-merer/resumen.texto: Records on papyrus, the oldest known texts with writing, written by Merer, a mid-level inspector, in year 27 of Khufu, the year after the 13th livestock count, a figure that exceeds the 23 years the Turin Canon gives that reign. They document the transport by boat of limestone blocks from the Tura quarries to Giza.

fuentes/diario-de-merer/por_que_importa.texto: They show how the construction of the Great Pyramid was supplied, with data on logistics and personnel.

fuentes/papiros-de-abusir/autor.texto: Officials of the funerary temples at Abusir

fuentes/papiros-de-abusir/resumen.texto: Administrative archives of the funerary temples of Neferirkare, Neferefre, and Nyuserre at Abusir. The first were found in 1893 at Abu Gurab, next to Abusir, and later a Czech expedition found others belonging to Neferefre and to another queen.

fuentes/papiros-de-abusir/por_que_import.texto: They are the most extensive archival documents of the Old Kingdom on how a royal funerary cult was organized and maintained.

fuentes/decretos-de-coptos/resumen.texto: Eighteen decrees (a-r), from Pepi I and Pepi II (Sixth Dynasty) and from kings of the Eighth Dynasty, carved on stelae from the temple of Min at Coptos and found by Reinach and Weill in 1910-1911. They deal with the temple and its personnel; those of the Eighth Dynasty raise Shemay to governor and vizier of Upper Egypt.

fuentes/decretos-de-coptos/por_que_impor.texto: They show how the kings of the late Old Kingdom and the following period protected the privileges and exemptions of a temple in Upper Egypt.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-sabni/resumen.texto: Biographical inscription on the facade of the tomb of Sabni at Qubbet el-Hawa. It recounts his expeditions to Nubia, where he recovered the body of his father Mekhu, who had died there on an earlier expedition.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-sabni/por_que_i.texto: It provides information on Egyptian expeditions to Nubia under Pepi II.

fuentes/autobiografia-de-sabni/leer.0.ti.texto: Translation by J. H. Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt, vol. I (1906), on Internet Archive

fuentes/inscripciones-de-tefibi/titulo.texto: Biography of Tefibi (Tomb III of Asyut)

fuentes/inscripciones-de-tefibi/resumen.texto: Biographical text carved in Tomb III of Asyut, of Tefibi, nomarch of the Tenth Dynasty and high priest of Wepwawet. It is the main source on his life.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-tefibi/por_que_.texto: It shows how a nomarch of Asyut presented himself before the kings of Herakleopolis, in the context of the war against Thebes.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ibi/titulo.texto: Inscriptions of the Tomb of Ibi at Deir el-Gabrawi

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ibi/resumen.texto: Chapel and shafts of the rock-cut tomb of Ibi, nomarch at the end of the Sixth Dynasty, who holds a large number of titles: member of the elite, royal sealer, and priest of the funerary temple of Pepi II.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-ibi/por_que_imp.texto: It is evidence of the power of the nomarchs toward the end of the Old Kingdom.

personas/iry-hor/resumen.texto: Ruler of Dynasty 0 (c. 3200-3000 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king), with serekhs at Abydos, Tell el-Farkha, and Zawyet el-Aryan, and an inscription found in 2012 at Wadi Ameyra, in Sinai, which also names Memphis. He is cited as the oldest Egyptian ruler known by name; until 2012 it was debated whether he was a king, and the Sinai inscription convinced most scholars.

personas/ka-sekhen/resumen.texto: King of Upper Egypt of Dynasty 0 (c. 3200-3000 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king); he is considered the immediate predecessor of Narmer. The length of his reign is unknown.

personas/escorpion-i/resumen.texto: Ruler of Upper Egypt during Naqada III, earlier than the span of Dynasty 0 in Shaw's chronology, 2000 (the year comes from the dating of Tomb U-j, around 3300 BC). A graffito depicting a battle is attributed to him, and, with doubts, Tomb U-j at Umm el-Qaab, from which the early evidence of wine consumption in Egypt comes.

personas/escorpion-ii/resumen.texto: Ruler of Upper Egypt of Dynasty 0 (c. 3200-3000 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king), known above all from the Hierakonpolis macehead, where a scorpion appears beside his figure. His Egyptian name is uncertain (Selk or Weha).

personas/ny-hor/resumen.texto: Possible predynastic king of Dynasty 0 (c. 3200-3000 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). His name, which according to Werner Kaiser means “the hunter,” is read in inscriptions, and his status as king is not certain.

personas/hat-hor/resumen.texto: Possible king of Dynasty 0, of the Naqada IIIB phase, known only from two inscriptions: one found in the eastern Nile Delta and another on a pottery sherd from Tura. His exact place of rule is unknown.

personas/hedju-hor/resumen.texto: Ruler of northern Egypt in the predynastic period, whose name means “the maces of Horus.” So little is known about him that historians debate what his social standing was.

personas/cocodrilo-rey/resumen.texto: Provisional name of a ruler from the end of Naqada III, who by one reading would have been a usurper in the time of Narmer. The reading of the few ink inscriptions, drawn carelessly, and with it his very existence, are much debated; his tomb is not known.

personas/doble-halcon/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lower Egypt during Naqada III, in the 32nd century BC according to estimates. The length of his reign is unknown.

personas/aha/resumen.texto: King whom most Egyptologists consider the second of the First Dynasty, and who in Shaw's chronology, 2000 opens the dynasty (3000-2890 BC, with no years per king); some identify him with Menes. He is believed to have had a long reign.

personas/neithhotep/resumen.texto: Woman of the court in the early First Dynasty, around 3050 BC, buried in a very large mastaba at Naqada. She is usually considered the wife of Narmer and the mother of Aha; some hold that she ruled in her own right.

personas/benerib/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the First Dynasty (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), from the time of Aha. Her name means “sweet of heart.”

personas/herneith/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the early First Dynasty (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000). Her name means “the face of Neith.”

personas/ahaneith/resumen.texto: Woman of the First Dynasty who gave her name to a stela found in Tomb Z at Umm el-Qaab, that of Djet (now in the Petrie Museum, London). It is unknown whether she was a wife, an official, or a relative of the king.

personas/djer/resumen.texto: Third king of the First Dynasty according to current Egyptology, with a reign of about four decades within the dynasty (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). His tomb at Umm el-Qaab has about 338 subsidiary burials; in it a mummified forearm was found, belonging to Djer or to his wife, which Émile Brugsch ruled out.

personas/penebui/resumen.texto: Queen of the First Dynasty, probable wife of Djer, whose name is engraved on several ivory tags. Helck proposed that she is the figure who appears in the sacrificial rite of year 4 of Djer's reign.

personas/djet/resumen.texto: Fourth king of the First Dynasty, successor of Djer (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). His Horus name means “Horus Cobra.”

personas/merneith/resumen.texto: Royal consort and regent of the First Dynasty, buried at Umm el-Qaab, around 2950 BC. Some consider her the first woman to rule in her own name, and she was the mother of Den.

personas/den/resumen.texto: King of the First Dynasty, the best documented archaeologically of his period, with a long reign (3000-2890 BC is the frame of the dynasty in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). His tomb at Umm el-Qaab has the oldest known granite floor in Egypt.

personas/seshemetka/resumen.texto: Queen of the First Dynasty, wife of Den, of whom very little is known beyond a stela found next to the king's tomb at Abydos. Wolfram Grajetzki, by contrast, gives her as the wife of Djer.

personas/semat/resumen.texto: Queen of the First Dynasty, wife of Den, buried near him at Abydos. Only one stela found next to the king's tomb is known; it was in the Berlin Museum and was destroyed in the Second World War.

personas/anedjib/resumen.texto: King of the First Dynasty (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). Manetho gives him 26 years of reign and the Turin Canon 74; Egyptologists attribute between 8 and 10 to him.

personas/betrest/resumen.texto: Queen of the First Dynasty (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), also read as Batyires or Batires. Very little is known about her.

personas/hemaka/resumen.texto: Senior official of the long reign of Den, in the First Dynasty, with the title of sealer of the king of Lower Egypt, that is, chancellor and second in power after the king. His name appears on many objects from mastaba S3035 at Saqqara, which is therefore usually considered his tomb.

personas/semerkhet/resumen.texto: King of the First Dynasty (3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king), with a reign of about eight and a half years. Manetho tells that a calamity occurred under him, and the legitimacy of his succession is debated.

personas/khenthap/resumen.texto: Possible queen of the First Dynasty who appears only once, in a much later inscription, with no sources from her own time. It is unknown which king she married; the date is an estimate within the dynasty.

personas/sabef/resumen.texto: Official of King Qa'a, in the First Dynasty, known from a stela found next to the king's tomb at Abydos.

personas/qaa/resumen.texto: Last king of the First Dynasty, with a reign of about 33 years by estimates, who in Shaw's chronology, 2000 closes the dynasty (3000-2890 BC, with no years per king).

personas/sneferka/resumen.texto: Short-lived king who may have reigned at the end of the First Dynasty; the length of his reign is unknown, but it is presumed to have been very brief, and his chronological position is unclear.

personas/pajaro-de-horus/resumen.texto: Possible king who may have had a very short reign between the First and Second Dynasties. His burial place is not known.

personas/ba-rey/resumen.texto: Serekh name of an ancient king whose position is unknown: he may have reigned at the end of the First Dynasty, in the late Second, or in the Third. The length of his reign and his chronology are unknown, and the date is only an estimate.

personas/hotepsekhemwy/resumen.texto: Founder of the Second Dynasty (2890-2686 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). Egyptologists attribute 25 or 29 years of reign to him; the Turin Canon gives 95 and Manetho 38. His tomb is at Saqqara.

personas/nebra/resumen.texto: Second king of the Second Dynasty (2890-2686 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king). Egyptologists attribute between 10 and 14 years of reign to him.

personas/nynetjer/resumen.texto: Third king of the Second Dynasty (2890-2686 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king) and the best documented of its first part, with a reign of about 40 years. Toward the end of his reign a division of the state is suspected.

personas/weneg/resumen.texto: King of the Second Dynasty (2890-2686 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king), also called Uneg. His chronological position is clear, but the length of his reign and which of the kings with Horus names identified by archaeology corresponds to him are unknown.

personas/wadjenes/resumen.texto: Name of a king of the Second Dynasty (“fresh of tongue”) that appears in the Ramesside royal lists but is not attested as a royal name in his own time. Egyptologists try to link him with a known king with a Horus name.

personas/nubnefer/resumen.texto: Birth name of a king who may have reigned during the Second Dynasty. The length of his reign and his chronological position are unknown.

personas/senedj/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Second Dynasty, with an uncertain historical position; his name appears in the Ramesside royal lists. How long he reigned is unknown: the Turin Canon gives him 54 years and Manetho 41.

personas/peribsen/resumen.texto: King of the Second Dynasty (2890-2686 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king), of disputed position, who used Seth and not Horus as the patron god of his royal name; his tomb is at Umm el-Qaab.

personas/neferkasokar/resumen.texto: King of the Second Dynasty known only from later sources, such as the royal lists; no contemporary records of him have been found and his tomb is not known, so Memphis is only the capital of the period.

personas/hudjefa-i/resumen.texto: He is not a named king but the “erased” mark of the Turin Canon, which records him with 11 years of reign in the Second Dynasty; the Saqqara Tablet also has a gap in that place. “Hudjefa” indicates that the name was already missing from the document the scribe copied.

personas/sekhemib/resumen.texto: King of the Second Dynasty (2890-2686 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which gives no years per king), well attested by documents of his time but absent from later lists. It is debated whether he was the predecessor, successor, or co-regent of Peribsen.

personas/khasekhemwy/resumen.texto: Last king of the Second Dynasty, who in Shaw's chronology, 2000 ends in 2686 BC; he is credited with about 18 years of reign. He reunified Egypt around his year 13 and raised the mudbrick structure of Shunet el-Zebib. He was buried at Umm el-Qaab.

personas/nebka/resumen.texto: King of the Third Dynasty (2686-2613 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), whom the lists and Manetho place as the founder of the dynasty; many identify him with Sanakht. His name appears in the tomb of a priest of his cult, almost contemporary, and perhaps in a cartouche from Beit Khallaf.

personas/nimaathap/resumen.texto: Consort queen at the transition from the Second to the Third Dynasty, mother of Djoser, of whom she may have been regent. She had a long-lasting funerary cult.

personas/sanakht/resumen.texto: King of the Third Dynasty (2686-2613 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), whose position is debated: many identify him with Nebka, the first of the dynasty in Shaw. The evidence consists of his reliefs on rocks at Wadi Maghara, in Sinai, since his tomb is not known.

personas/djoser/resumen.texto: King of the Third Dynasty, son of Khasekhemwy and Nimaathap, who reigned c. 2667-2648 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He is associated with the Step Pyramid of Saqqara, the first great stone building in Egypt.

personas/inetkaes/resumen.texto: Princess of the Third Dynasty, the only known daughter of King Djoser and Queen Hetephernebti. She is named on the boundary stelae surrounding the Step Pyramid and appears in a relief from Heliopolis, now in Turin.

personas/hetephernebti/resumen.texto: Queen of the Third Dynasty, the only known wife of Djoser, named on stelae found next to his pyramid complex at Saqqara and on a relief from Heliopolis.

personas/hetepi/resumen.texto: Official of King Djoser, in the Third Dynasty, known from his monumental tomb at South Abusir, discovered by a Czech expedition in 1999-2000. The mudbrick mastaba is almost 50 m long and has a limestone chapel.

personas/hesy-ra/resumen.texto: Senior official of the Third Dynasty, under Djoser, whose title is read as “greatest of the ivory carvers” or “of the dentists”; if the reading is “of the dentists,” he would be the oldest dentist known by name. His tomb at Saqqara preserves cedar panels.

personas/akhetaa/resumen.texto: Senior official of the Third Dynasty, known from the inscriptions of his tomb, which cite rarely used titles and King Nebka, in whose cult he served.

personas/sekhemkhet/resumen.texto: King of the Third Dynasty, perhaps a brother or son of Djoser, who reigned c. 2648-2640 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He left an unfinished Step Pyramid, the “Buried Pyramid.”

personas/khaba/resumen.texto: King of the Third Dynasty (2686-2613 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), almost certainly toward the end of the dynasty; his name is on stone vessels and clay seals. The Layer Pyramid at Zawyet el-Aryan is tentatively attributed to him.

personas/huni/resumen.texto: Last king of the Third Dynasty, who reigned c. 2637-2613 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000); the Turin Canon gives him 24 years of reign.

personas/metjen/resumen.texto: Senior official at the transition between the Third and Fourth Dynasties; the inscription in his tomb says that he served under Huni and Snefru.

personas/pehernefer/resumen.texto: Senior official who held offices under Huni and Snefru, at the transition from the Third to the Fourth Dynasty. An estate of Meresankh, mother of Snefru, may be named in his tomb at Saqqara.

personas/meresankh-i/resumen.texto: Royal wife and mother of Snefru; she may have been a wife of Huni, the last king of the Third Dynasty. Her name appears on a fragment of the Palermo Stone and, together with that of her son, in graffiti from the Meidum temple from the time of Thutmose III.

personas/snefru/resumen.texto: First king of the Fourth Dynasty, who reigned c. 2613-2589 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He is credited with the Meidum Pyramid (which Huni may have begun), the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid at Dahshur, as well as the small pyramid at Seila.

personas/hetepheres-i/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, wife of Snefru and mother of Khufu. Her burial equipment was found in 1925 in shaft G 7000x, next to the pyramid of Khufu; the sarcophagus was empty, and Reisner interpreted this as a reburial.

personas/nefermaat/resumen.texto: Prince and son of Snefru, vizier with the titles of eldest son of the king and royal sealer. His tomb is at Meidum.

personas/rahotep-principe/resumen.texto: Prince of the Fourth Dynasty, son of Snefru and of his first wife Hetepheres I, although other authors doubt the filiation. He is known from his mastaba 6 at Meidum and from the statues of Rahotep and his wife Nofret, now in the Cairo Museum.

personas/kanefer/resumen.texto: Prince, son of Snefru, who held the office of vizier after his elder brother Nefermaat; the office then passed to Hemiunu.

personas/khufu/resumen.texto: Second king of the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2589-2566 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He is credited with the Great Pyramid of Giza; his reign is poorly documented, and he appears in the Westcar Papyrus.

personas/meritites-i/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, daughter of Snefru and wife of Khufu, with whom she was the mother of Prince Kawab. She was buried in the central queens' pyramid at Giza.

personas/henutsen/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, second or third wife of Khufu, probably buried at Giza.

personas/hemiunu/resumen.texto: Prince and vizier of Khufu, believed to be the architect of the Great Pyramid, and supervisor of the royal works. His tomb is in the western cemetery at Giza.

personas/kawab/resumen.texto: Prince of the Fourth Dynasty, eldest son of Khufu and Meritites I, who was a vizier. He is buried in the double mastaba G 7110-7120 at Giza.

personas/nefertiabet/resumen.texto: Princess of the Fourth Dynasty, perhaps a daughter of Khufu or more probably a daughter of Snefru. Her stela from the tomb at Giza, now in the Louvre, is dated to about 2580 BC.

personas/djedefhor/resumen.texto: Noble of the Fourth Dynasty and son of Khufu, whose name means “enduring like Horus.” Later tradition attributes to him a teaching (the Instruction of Hordjedef); he appears in the Westcar Papyrus, and the Harper's Song names him alongside Imhotep.

personas/khufukhaf-i/resumen.texto: Prince and vizier of the Fourth Dynasty, son of Khufu, full brother of Khafre and half-brother of Djedefre, who held office perhaps toward the end of Khufu's reign or under Khafre. His double mastaba, G 7130-7140, is in the eastern cemetery at Giza, and he shares it with his wife Nefertkau II.

personas/minkhaf-i/resumen.texto: Prince of the Fourth Dynasty, son of Khufu, half-brother of Djedefre and elder brother of Khafre; he was vizier, probably under Khufu or Khafre.

personas/meritites-ii/resumen.texto: Princess of the Fourth Dynasty, probably a daughter of Khufu, active around 2550 BC; she may have been a daughter of Meritites I, named in mastaba G 7650.

personas/djedefre/resumen.texto: King of the Fourth Dynasty, son and successor of Khufu, c. 2566-2558 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He introduced the title “son of Ra” and built his pyramid at Abu Rawash.

personas/hetepheres-ii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, daughter of Khufu, wife of Kawab and then of Djedefre, and mother of Queen Meresankh III.

personas/neferhetepes/resumen.texto: Princess of the Fourth Dynasty, daughter of Djedefre, who reigned between Khufu and Khafre, and of Hetepheres II.

personas/khafre/resumen.texto: Fourth king of the Fourth Dynasty, son of Khufu and successor of Djedefre, c. 2558-2532 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He is credited with his pyramid at Giza and, according to a common attribution, the Great Sphinx.

personas/khamerernebty-i/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, probable wife of Khafre and mother of Menkaure and of Queen Khamerernebty II. She may have been a daughter of Khufu.

personas/persenet/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, perhaps a daughter of Khufu and wife of Khafre. She is known above all from her tomb at Giza, G 8156.

personas/hekenuhedjet/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, wife of Khafre, depicted in the tomb of her son, the vizier Sekhemkare. She is shown seated behind him, with an arm over his shoulders; the damaged text calls her great favorite and priestess.

personas/meresankh-ii/resumen.texto: Consort queen of Egypt during the Fourth Dynasty, around 2550 BC. Her name means “she loves life.”

personas/meresankh-iii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, daughter of Kawab and Hetepheres II and wife of Khafre. Her tomb at Giza was excavated by George Reisner in 1927.

personas/nebemakhet/resumen.texto: Prince and vizier of the Fourth Dynasty, son of Khafre and Meresankh III; he appears in his mother's tomb and in his own at Giza.

personas/rekhetre/resumen.texto: Queen of the late Fourth or early Fifth Dynasty, daughter of Khafre. Her husband is never mentioned; he would have been one of Khafre's successors, perhaps Menkaure.

personas/khamerernebty-ii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth Dynasty, daughter of Khafre and Khamerernebty I and wife of her brother Menkaure, with whom she was the mother of Prince Khuenre.

personas/duaenre/resumen.texto: Vizier of Menkaure, in the Fourth Dynasty, with the titles of son of the king of his body, hereditary prince, and scribe of the divine book.

personas/seneb/resumen.texto: High-ranking official of the Fourth Dynasty, a dwarf, owner of thousands of head of cattle, and married to a high-ranking priestess, with whom he had three children. His family appears in a painted sculptural group from his tomb, rediscovered in 1926.

personas/menkaure/resumen.texto: King of the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2532-2503 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His pyramid is the third at Giza.

personas/nikaure/resumen.texto: Prince and vizier of the Fourth Dynasty, probably under Menkaure; his title includes that of eldest son of the king and chief of justice.

personas/bikheris/resumen.texto: Hellenized name of a king who may have reigned during the Fourth Dynasty and who is attested only by Manetho. So little is known about him that some Egyptologists believe he is fictitious.

personas/baufra/resumen.texto: Supposed son of King Khufu, of the Fourth Dynasty, known from an account in the Westcar Papyrus and from a rock inscription in Wadi Hammamat. He is not attested in his own time or by archaeology, and specialists debate whether he existed.

personas/bunefer/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fourth or Fifth Dynasty, with no known king as her husband, buried in tomb G 8408 in the central field of Giza.

personas/kaaper/resumen.texto: Scribe and priest from the late Fourth or early Fifth Dynasty, of not very high rank but famous for his very finely made wooden statue, known as “Sheikh el-Beled.”

personas/ankhhaf/resumen.texto: Prince of the Fourth Dynasty, supervisor under Khufu, of whom he is believed to be a half-brother; some of his titles include vizier, but it is not known under which king. The Diary of Merer names him as the noble in charge of the works, and his painted limestone bust is in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

personas/shepseskaf/resumen.texto: Last king of the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2503-2498 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with a probable reign of four years. He had himself buried in the Mastabat al-Fir'aun, in South Saqqara.

personas/thamphthis/resumen.texto: Hellenized name of an ephemeral ruler at the end of the Fourth Dynasty (2613-2494 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), perhaps called Djedefptah or Djedefkaf. His original Egyptian name was lost, and he has no contemporary attestation.

personas/userkaf/resumen.texto: Founder of the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2494-2487 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). He built his pyramid at Saqqara and a sun temple between Abusir and Abu Gurab.

personas/khentkaus-i/resumen.texto: Royal woman between the Fourth and Fifth Dynasties, perhaps a daughter of Menkaure, wife of Shepseskaf and of Userkaf, and mother of Sahure. It is debated whether she was a regent or even ruled in her own right; her mastaba is next to Menkaure's at Giza.

personas/neferhetepes-esposa-de-userkaf/.texto: Queen of the Fifth Dynasty, mother of Sahure and very probably wife of Userkaf, the first king of the dynasty. She died around 2480 BC.

personas/sahure/resumen.texto: Second king of the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2487-2475 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His pyramid began the use of Abusir as a royal necropolis.

personas/meretnebty/resumen.texto: Consort queen of Sahure, around 2485 BC, mother of Neferirkare Kakai.

personas/neferirkare/resumen.texto: Third king of the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2475-2455 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His funerary temple produced the Abusir Papyri.

personas/washptah/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Fifth Dynasty under Neferirkare, c. 2470 BC. His mastaba in northern Saqqara carries a biography about an illness he suffered before the king.

personas/khentkaus-ii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fifth Dynasty, wife of Neferirkare and mother of the kings Neferefre and Nyuserre.

personas/shepseskare/resumen.texto: King of the Fifth Dynasty who, in Shaw's chronology, 2000 reigned c. 2455-2448 BC, between Neferirkare and Neferefre. Verner holds that he reigned for a few months after Neferefre, and Nuzzolo (2022) places him after Nyuserre.

personas/neferefre/resumen.texto: King of the Fifth Dynasty with a very brief reign, probably two years or less, c. 2448-2445 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). His pyramid at Abusir was left unfinished.

personas/khentkaus-iii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fifth Dynasty, probable daughter of Neferirkare and Khentkaus II and wife of Neferefre, and mother of the future king Menkauhor Kaiu. Her tomb was found by a Czech expedition, and the press sometimes called her Khentakawess III.

personas/nyuserre/resumen.texto: Sixth king of the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2445-2421 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). Youngest son of Neferirkare and Khentkaus II, he built the sun temple of Abu Gurab and a pyramid at Abusir.

personas/ptahshepses/resumen.texto: Vizier and son-in-law of Nyuserre Ini during the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2450 BC; his mastaba complex at Abusir is considered the largest private tomb of the Old Kingdom.

personas/seshemnefer-iii/resumen.texto: Vizier in the time of Nyuserre Ini, in the Fifth Dynasty, the third of his family to hold the office. His tomb G 5170 is on the western side of the pyramid of Khufu, and its decorations provide information on his life and his ancestors.

personas/reptynub/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fifth Dynasty, wife of Nyuserre Ini and possible mother of Menkauhor Kaiu.

personas/niankhkhnum-y-khnumhotep/resume.texto: Two royal servants who shared the title of overseer of the palace manicurists of Nyuserre Ini and were buried together at Saqqara. Altenmüller considers them brothers, Baines twins, and Reeder a couple; this last reading, of the oldest known same-sex couple, is the most often cited.

personas/khufukhaf-ii/resumen.texto: Senior official of the Old Kingdom, probably born in the Fourth Dynasty and died under Nyuserre Ini, in the Fifth. He is also called Khufukhaf B or the Younger to distinguish him from Khufukhaf I, his probable father or grandfather.

personas/menkauhor/resumen.texto: King of the Fifth Dynasty, successor of Nyuserre, with a reign of about eight or nine years (c. 2421-2414 BC, Shaw's chronology, 2000). The so-called Decapitated Pyramid of Saqqara is tentatively attributed to him.

personas/djedkare/resumen.texto: King of the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2414-2375 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with a long reign of about 39 years. He built a pyramid in South Saqqara.

personas/rashepses/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Fifth Dynasty under Djedkare Isesi, c. 2400 BC; his tomb at Saqqara preserves the text of a royal letter addressed to him.

personas/senedjemib-inti/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Fifth Dynasty during the reign of Djedkare Isesi, died around 2375 BC.

personas/ptahhotep-tjefi/resumen.texto: Vizier at the end of the Fifth Dynasty, probably under Djedkare Isesi and Unas, son of the vizier Akhethotep; his double mastaba at Saqqara was built for him and his father. He is Ptahhotep II, grandson of the vizier Ptahhotep I, and not the Ptahhotep to whom the Teaching is attributed.

personas/unas/resumen.texto: Last king of the Fifth Dynasty, c. 2375-2345 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with a reign of about 30 years. The oldest known Pyramid Texts were carved in his pyramid.

personas/nebet-esposa-de-unas/resumen.texto: Queen of the Fifth Dynasty, wife of Unas; she is considered the mother of the crown prince Unas-ankh, a disputed point.

personas/khenut/resumen.texto: Consort queen of Unas, around 2360 BC, suspected of being the mother of Queen Iput.

personas/ihy-visir/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Fifth Dynasty, in office most probably under Unas, with titles of supervisor of the treasuries, of the royal works, and of the double granary. His mastaba next to the pyramid of Unas was usurped by Teti's daughter Seshseshet Idut; only his sarcophagus preserves his name.

personas/teti/resumen.texto: First king of the Sixth Dynasty, buried at Saqqara, who reigned c. 2345-2323 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), about 22 years; the Turin Canon's number of years for his reign is destroyed.

personas/sesheshet/resumen.texto: Mother of King Teti, to whom a role is attributed in his accession to the throne and in the reconciliation of two factions of the royal family. In 2008 what is believed to be her pyramid was found.

personas/iput-i/resumen.texto: Queen of the Sixth Dynasty, daughter of Unas and wife of Teti, mother of Pepi I and a possible regent for him.

personas/khuit-ii/resumen.texto: Wife of Teti, first king of the Sixth Dynasty, around 2340 BC.

personas/kagemni/resumen.texto: Vizier at the beginning of Teti's reign, around 2345 BC, married to a daughter of the king, Seshseshet Nubkhetnebty; his mastaba is the largest in Teti's cemetery. He should not be confused with the Kagemni of the Instruction, whom tradition places under Huni and Snefru.

personas/mereruka/resumen.texto: Vizier of Teti and husband of his daughter Seshseshet Waatetkhethor; his mastaba at Saqqara, with 33 rooms, is the largest private tomb in the necropolis. The office of vizier placed him below the king alone.

personas/mehu/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Sixth Dynasty whose exact date is debated: Altenmüller places him under Teti. His large mastaba at Saqqara is near the pyramid of Unas.

personas/merefnebef/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Sixth Dynasty, also called Unisankh and Fefi, who served at the court of Teti; he may have been vizier under Userkare and was dismissed under Pepi I.

personas/userkare/resumen.texto: Second king of the Sixth Dynasty, who reigned c. 2323-2321 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000); his relationship with Teti and Pepi I is unknown. Manetho does not mention him, but the Abydos King List does.

personas/pepi-i/resumen.texto: Third king of the Sixth Dynasty, who reigned c. 2321-2287 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), more than 40 years. Son of Teti, he came to the throne after the brief reign of Userkare.

personas/ankhesenpepi-i/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the Sixth Dynasty, wife of Pepi I and mother of Merenre Nemtyemsaf I.

personas/ankhesenpepi-ii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Sixth Dynasty, wife of Pepi I and of Merenre, mother of Pepi II, of whom she was probably regent during his minority. She is buried in a pyramid at Saqqara.

personas/inenek-inti/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the Sixth Dynasty, wife of Pepi I, with her own pyramid near that of her husband in South Saqqara.

personas/nubwenet/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the Sixth Dynasty, one of the wives of Pepi I.

personas/nedjeftet/resumen.texto: Queen of the Sixth Dynasty mentioned in reliefs near the pyramid complex of Pepi I; she may have been one of his wives. Her name is that of the 20th nome of Upper Egypt, from where her family perhaps came.

personas/merenre-i/resumen.texto: Fourth king of the Sixth Dynasty, c. 2287-2278 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000); son of Pepi I. Under him Harkhuf carried out expeditions to Nubia.

personas/weni/resumen.texto: Official of the Sixth Dynasty who served under Teti, Pepi I, and Merenre. His autobiography carved in his tomb recounts the campaigns he led against the peoples of the east and the quarrying expeditions; he has a second tomb in the necropolis of Pepi I, at Saqqara, with an almost identical copy of the biography.

personas/harkhuf/resumen.texto: Native official of Elephantine, governor of Upper Egypt under Merenre and Pepi II. His tomb at Qubbet el-Hawa has the autobiography in which he narrates four great expeditions to Yam, in Nubia.

personas/djau/resumen.texto: Vizier of Upper Egypt of the Sixth Dynasty, from an influential family of Abydos; he was the maternal uncle of Pepi II, and was already vizier when Pepi II came to the throne. He appears in decrees from Abydos and Coptos.

personas/behenu/resumen.texto: Queen of the Sixth Dynasty, believed to be a wife of Pepi I or of Pepi II.

personas/pepi-ii/resumen.texto: King of the Sixth Dynasty who came to the throne at the age of six and reigned c. 2278-2184 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). The documents of his time reach his year 62, so the 90 or 94 years of Manetho and the Canon are doubtful; the power of the nomarchs grew during his reign, and the Old Kingdom broke up shortly afterward.

personas/iput-ii/resumen.texto: Consort queen of the Sixth Dynasty, sister and wife of Pepi II.

personas/neith-esposa-de-pepi-ii/resumen.texto: One of the principal queens of Pepi II, with her own pyramid at Saqqara.

personas/ankhesenpepi-iii/resumen.texto: Queen of the Sixth Dynasty, daughter of Merenre Nemtyemsaf I and wife of Pepi II, probably her uncle; she was buried in a pyramid next to that of Pepi I.

personas/ankhesenpepi-iv/resumen.texto: Wife of Pepi II, in the Sixth Dynasty, and mother of the crown prince Neferkare. The lid of her sarcophagus bears on its reverse the South Saqqara Stone, an annalistic text of the kings of the Sixth Dynasty.

personas/udjebten/resumen.texto: Consort queen of Pepi II, around 2250 BC.

personas/heqaib/resumen.texto: Nomarch of the first nome of Upper Egypt under Pepi II, around 2250 BC, in charge of military expeditions to Nubia. After his death he was deified.

personas/sabni/resumen.texto: Official of Pepi II who led expeditions to Nubia; his biography is on the facade of his tomb at Qubbet el-Hawa.

personas/qar/resumen.texto: Vizier of the Sixth Dynasty whose funerary complex was found at Abusir in 1995 by a Czech expedition; he had four children, among them Senedjemib.

personas/merenre-ii/resumen.texto: Penultimate king of the Sixth Dynasty, who reigned one year and one month, perhaps already elderly, after Pepi II (around 2184 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, which does not list him separately).

personas/ibi-nomarca/resumen.texto: Nomarch at the end of the Sixth Dynasty, of the 8th nome of Upper Egypt (Ta-wer) and of the 12th (Diospolis Parva), known from his rock-cut tomb at Deir el-Gabrawi, in the latter; he was a priest of the funerary temple of Pepi II.

personas/netjerkare-siptah/resumen.texto: Seventh and last king of the Sixth Dynasty; for some he is the first of the Seventh or the Eighth; he is sometimes considered the last king of the Old Kingdom. He reigned c. 2184-2181 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000).

personas/nitocris/resumen.texto: Queen whom Herodotus and Manetho place at the end of the Sixth Dynasty. According to Herodotus, she avenged her brother by inviting his murderers to a banquet and drowning them by flooding the hall. Ryholt holds that the name “Neitiqerty” in the Turin Canon corresponds to Netjerkare Siptah, misread, and that the queen is legendary, so no reign of her own is assigned to her.

personas/menkare/resumen.texto: King who may have been the first or second of the Eighth Dynasty, perhaps with a brief reign at the transition between the Old Kingdom and the First Intermediate Period, in the 22nd century BC. The rapid succession of short reigns suggests hard times, which some link to the climatic event of 2200 BC.

personas/neferkare-neby/resumen.texto: King of the Seventh or Eighth Dynasty who appears as the fourth king of the Seventh Dynasty in the Abydos King List. Two sources from his own time also attest him: the false door and the sarcophagus of Queen Ankhesenpepi II, which would make him her son and perhaps Merenre's.

personas/djedkare-shemai/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Eighth Dynasty, known only from the Abydos King List; he is missing from the Turin Canon, where a gap affects most of the kings of the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties. No document or building from his time bearing his name has been found.

personas/neferkare-khendu/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty, the sixth of it according to Ryholt, Beckerath, and Baker, attested only by the Abydos King List; he is missing from the Turin Canon, where a gap affects most of the kings of the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties.

personas/merenhor/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Eighth Dynasty, known only from the Abydos King List; he is missing from the Turin Canon, where a gap affects most of the kings of the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties. No document or building from his time bearing his name has been found.

personas/neferkamin/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Eighth Dynasty. His name appears only in the Abydos King List, perhaps through a copying error, and a gold plaque in the British Museum has it next to that of Nikare, although it is suspected to be a forgery.

personas/nikare/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Eighth Dynasty, the ninth of it according to Ryholt, Beckerath, and Baker, with his seat of power at Memphis.

personas/neferkare-tereru/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Eighth Dynasty, known only from the Abydos King List; he is missing from the Turin Canon. No document or building from his time bearing his name has been found.

personas/qakare-ibi/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty (2181-2160 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, with no years per king), with his seat at Memphis, with a reign of about two years according to the Turin Canon; he probably did not rule all of Egypt. He is among the best attested of his dynasty, through his small pyramid in South Saqqara.

personas/neferkahor/resumen.texto: King who may have reigned during the Eighth Dynasty, the eleventh of it according to Beckerath and Baker, known from the Abydos King List and from a steatite cylinder seal of unknown provenance.

personas/neferkare-pepiseneb/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty, the twelfth of it according to Ryholt, Beckerath, and Baker, during the beginning of the First Intermediate Period.

personas/neferkamin-anu/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty, the thirteenth of it according to the Abydos King List and Ryholt's reconstruction of the Turin Canon, who would have ruled the Memphis region.

personas/neferkaure/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty, the fifteenth of it according to the Abydos King List and the latest reconstruction of the Turin Canon, with his seat at Memphis; he may not have had power over all of Egypt.

personas/wadjkare/resumen.texto: Possible king of the Eighth Dynasty (2181-2160 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), a very obscure figure of Egyptian history, who appears only in Decree R from Coptos. Some doubt his existence.

personas/shemay/resumen.texto: Official and later vizier toward the end of the Eighth Dynasty, known as the beneficiary of most of the Coptos decrees. His career is interpreted as a sign of the weakness of central power, which had to grant great privileges to keep local governors loyal; he is buried in a mudbrick mastaba south of Coptos.

personas/idy/resumen.texto: Senior official of the Eighth Dynasty, son of Shemay and vizier, known from several sources; Decree R from Coptos deals only with his welfare.

personas/neferkauhor/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty, the sixteenth and penultimate, who reigned a little over two years with a probable seat in the Memphis region. He is among the best attested of his time, with eight decrees surviving in fragments.

personas/tjauti/resumen.texto: Official at the end of the Eighth Dynasty, nomarch of the Coptos nome. He appears in rock inscriptions at Gebel Tjauti and in fragments of a false door found near Khozam, and his capital, Coptos, is only the nearest place documented.

personas/neferirkare-pepi-iii/resumen.texto: King of the Eighth Dynasty, the seventeenth and last according to Ryholt, Beckerath, and Baker; many regard him as the last king of the Old Kingdom. In Shaw's numbering the Eighth Dynasty ends in 2160 BC.

personas/khui/resumen.texto: King or nomarch of the early First Intermediate Period, whom Beckerath proposes as a king of the Eighth Dynasty, and who may have been a provincial governor who proclaimed himself king. The pyramid of Dara is attributed to him.

personas/meryibre-khety/resumen.texto: King of the Ninth or Tenth Dynasty during the First Intermediate Period, one of the two candidates for founder of the dynasty (Manetho's Aktoes), around 2160 BC.

personas/imhotep-rey/resumen.texto: Short-lived ruler who probably reigned in the Ninth Dynasty or perhaps the Tenth, known from two rock inscriptions in Wadi Hammamat.

personas/neferkare-vii/resumen.texto: Third king of the Ninth Dynasty according to the Turin Canon, around 2140 BC; only the Turin Canon names him, and it is debated whether he is the Kaneferre of the tomb of Anjtifi.

personas/neferu-i/resumen.texto: First consort queen of the Eleventh Dynasty, perhaps a wife of Mentuhotep I, mother of Intef I and Intef II, and grandmother of Intef III and of Queen Iah.

personas/wahkare-khety/resumen.texto: King of the First Intermediate Period whose position is debated: founder of the Ninth Dynasty (Manetho's cruel Aktoes) or king of the Tenth, father of Merikare and supposed author of his Instruction. According to that Instruction he retook Tinis with Tefibi of Asyut, and his troops plundered the necropolis.

personas/nebkaure-khety/resumen.texto: King of the Ninth or Tenth Dynasty during the First Intermediate Period.

personas/neferkare-viii/resumen.texto: Second king of the Tenth Dynasty (2160-2025 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, with no years per king), attested only by the Turin Canon. His throne name suggests that he considered himself the legitimate successor of Pepi II Neferkare.

personas/tefibi/resumen.texto: Nomarch of Asyut in the Tenth Dynasty (21st century BC), high priest of Wepwawet. His biography is inscribed in Tomb III of Asyut.

personas/meryhathor/resumen.texto: King of the Tenth Dynasty during the First Intermediate Period (2160-2025 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, with no years per king).

personas/khety-ii/resumen.texto: Nomarch of the 13th nome of Upper Egypt, that of Asyut, son of Tefibi. Merikare installed him in office, restored works at the temple of Wepwawet, and remained loyal to the Tenth Dynasty to the end; his unfinished tomb at Asyut (IV) is the only one of his family that mentions a royal name, that of Merikare.

personas/merikare/resumen.texto: King of the Tenth Dynasty, toward the end of the First Intermediate Period (before 2025 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000), seated at Herakleopolis, who maintained a relatively peaceful coexistence with the Theban rulers of the Eleventh Dynasty. The text of the “Instruction for Merikare” is addressed to him.

personas/ankhtifi/resumen.texto: Nomarch of Hierakonpolis, a supporter of the kings of Herakleopolis, who fought against Thebes at the beginning of the First Intermediate Period. His tomb at Moalla narrates his campaigns and his aid during the famine.

personas/intef-el-anciano/resumen.texto: Nomarch of Thebes during the First Intermediate Period, around 2150 BC, later considered a founding figure of the Eleventh Dynasty.

personas/mentuhotep-i/resumen.texto: Possible nomarch of Thebes and independent ruler of Upper Egypt before 2125 BC, when the Theban Eleventh Dynasty begins in Shaw's chronology, 2000. Another hypothesis considers him a figure created later, under Intef II and Mentuhotep II, as the founder of the dynasty.

personas/intef-i/resumen.texto: First member of the Eleventh Dynasty to use a Horus name, after being nomarch of Thebes; he reigned between 4 and 16 years, c. 2125-2112 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000, and probably fought against the Coptite nomarch Tjauti. He is buried at El-Tarif.

personas/intef-ii/resumen.texto: King of the Eleventh Dynasty, who ruled from Thebes c. 2112-2063 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000); he extended Theban authority to Lower Nubia and consolidated control of Upper Egypt.

personas/iah/resumen.texto: Queen of the Eleventh Dynasty, daughter of a king (perhaps Intef II), wife of Intef III and mother of Mentuhotep II; active around 2060 BC.

personas/intef-iii/resumen.texto: Third king of the Eleventh Dynasty, son of Intef II and father of Mentuhotep II, who reigned c. 2063-2055 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000) and extended Theban domination northward against the Tenth Dynasty.

hechos/naqada-iii/resumen.texto: Last phase of the Naqada culture, c. 3200-3000 BC (according to the sources, from 3325 to 3000), when the process of state formation begun in Naqada II becomes very visible, with named kings at the head of powerful kingdoms. It is often called the Protodynastic period.

hechos/cultura-de-maadi-buto/resumen.texto: Prehistoric culture of Lower Egypt, with about a dozen sites, among them the cemetery and settlement of Maadi, next to present-day Cairo. It is identified from the second part of Naqada I and continued until Naqada IIc/d, when the Naqada culture replaced it; other important sites are el-Gerza, Haraga, Abusir el-Melek, and Minshat Abu Omar.

hechos/reemplazo-de-la-cultura-de-maadi-.texto: The Naqada culture replaces the Maadi-Buto culture
By Naqada IIc/d the Naqada culture of Upper Egypt replaces the Maadi-Buto culture, which had predominated in Lower Egypt.

hechos/dinastia-0-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Kings of Egypt during Naqada III, c. 3200-3000 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), who wrote their names in serekhs on vessels and tombs. The period was marked by constant conflict with the peoples of the Delta, probably over control of trade routes with the Levant, and it ends with the legendary king Menes, who is usually associated with Narmer or Aha.

hechos/dinastia-1-de-egipto/resumen.texto: First series of kings of a unified Egypt, after the union of Upper and Lower Egypt by Menes or Narmer, with power centered at Tinis; it occupies c. 3000-2890 BC in Shaw's chronology, 2000. Estimates for its beginning range from the 34th to the 30th century BC; a 2013 radiocarbon dating placed the accession of Hor-Aha between 3111 and 3045 BC with 68 % confidence.

hechos/dinastia-2-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Second of the two dynasties of the Archaic period, with government centered at Tinis, c. 2890-2686 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000). It is very obscure except for its last king, Khasekhemwy; in it appear the first complete known sentences in hieroglyphs, such as the one on a seal from the tomb of Peribsen.

hechos/dinastia-3-de-egipto/resumen.texto: First dynasty of the Old Kingdom, c. 2686-2613 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with its capital at Memphis. After the turbulent final years of the Second Dynasty, which perhaps included a civil war, power passed to Djoser; the Turin Canon and the Abydos King List give five kings, the Saqqara Tablet four, and Manetho nine.

hechos/dinastia-4-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Golden age of the Old Kingdom, c. 2613-2494 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), with peace, prosperity, and officially documented foreign trade. The building experiments of Snefru led from the mastaba to the smooth-sided pyramids, such as those at Giza.

hechos/dinastia-5-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Dynasty of nine kings, from Userkaf to Unas, c. 2494-2345 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), about 150 years. The relative succession of the kings is not entirely certain, because of the contradictions between the historical sources and archaeology about the reign of Shepseskare.

hechos/dinastia-6-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Last dynasty of the Old Kingdom for many authors, c. 2345-2181 BC (Shaw's chronology, 2000), although the Oxford History includes the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties in the Old Kingdom as well. From the Fifth Dynasty onward the bureaucracy and the priesthood grew and royal power declined, and that decentralization continued under the kings of the Sixth.

hechos/dinastia-7-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Dynasty that according to Manetho marked the beginning of the First Intermediate Period, in the 22nd century BC (c. 2181-2160 BC, Shaw's chronology, 2000, which joins the Seventh and Eighth). Its existence is debated: Manetho presents it as a metaphor for chaos, Beckerath and Wilkinson consider it fictitious, and Papazian proposed in 2015 that it was real and that its kings are those usually attributed to the Eighth.

hechos/dinastia-8-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Little-known and brief dynasty of kings who succeeded one another quickly at the beginning of the 22nd century BC, probably seated at Memphis (c. 2181-2160 BC, Shaw's chronology, 2000). The power of the king declined against that of the nomarchs, notably those of Coptos, and the dynasty was overthrown by the nomarchs of Herakleopolis Magna, who founded the Ninth.

hechos/dinastia-9-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Dynasty founded at Herakleopolis Magna, which seems to have supplanted the Eighth (c. 2160-2025 BC together with the Tenth, Shaw's chronology, 2000). The seizure of power was violent, according to Manetho, who describes its founder, Aktoes, as more terrible than his predecessors; the Turin Canon lists 18 kings with damaged or lost names.

hechos/dinastia-10-de-egipto/resumen.texto: Continuation of the Ninth Dynasty at Herakleopolis Magna, with which it is usually grouped (c. 2160-2025 BC, Shaw's chronology, 2000). Egypt was not unified, and there was overlap with other local dynasties, among them the Theban one.

hechos/dinastia-11-tebana-de-egipto/resu.texto: Well-attested kings who governed from Thebes; those before Mentuhotep II count in the First Intermediate Period (c. 2125-2055 BC, Shaw's chronology, 2000), and the later ones in the Middle Kingdom. Manetho gives 16 kings in 43 years, but the inscriptions and the Turin Canon give seven kings who ruled 143 years.

hechos/tumba-u-j-de-abidos/resumen.texto: Twelve-chambered mudbrick tomb of Naqada IIIA2, the largest in the U cemetery, with wine, imported pottery, and 186 tags with proto-hieroglyphic signs. It is debated whether it belonged to Scorpion I or to a king called Bull; its excavator considered it royal.

hechos/gebelein-momias-predinasticas/tit.texto: Predynastic naturally mummified bodies from Gebelein

hechos/gebelein-momias-predinasticas/res.texto: Six naturally mummified bodies from sand graves at Gebelein, from the Late Predynastic period; the best known, EA 32751, is from Naqada II, around 3400 BC (calibrated range 3341 to 3017 BC). Wallis Budge excavated them in 1896, and the British Museum acquired them in 1900.

hechos/cuchillo-de-gebel-el-arak/resumen.texto: Ivory and flint knife from the end of Naqada II, with Mesopotamian influence, which the Louvre, where it is now, bought in Cairo in 1914. The seller said it came from Gebel el-Arak, but it is now believed to come from Abydos.

hechos/vestido-de-tarkhan/resumen.texto: Linen garment more than 5,000 years old, the oldest surviving piece of woven clothing, excavated in 1913 in the Tarkhan necropolis and now in the Petrie Museum, London. A 1978 radiocarbon dating had put it around 2362 BC, but a 2015 dating by the University of Oxford places it with 95 % certainty between 3482 and 3102 BC.

hechos/templo-de-satet-en-elefantina/res.texto: Temple of the goddess Satet, personification of the Nile flood, founded at the end of the Predynastic period, around 3200 BC, and enlarged and renovated several times from the Archaic period for about 3,000 years. It is the best example of an Egyptian temple whose construction is attested throughout the pharaonic period.

hechos/fundacion-de-menfis-segun-la-trad.texto: Foundation of Memphis attributed to Menes

Herodotus attributes the founding of Memphis to Menes, with a dike that diverted the Nile; Manetho attributes the palace of Memphis to Menes's son, Atothis. The Iry-Hor inscription from Wadi Ameyra, found in 2012, already names Memphis before Narmer, and Menes marks the beginning of the First Dynasty in Shaw's chronology, 2000.

hechos/tumbas-reales-de-umm-el-qaab/resu.texto: The kings of Dynasty 0 and of the First Dynasty up to Qa'a had tombs made at Umm el-Qaab, larger and more complex than the predynastic ones: cemetery B has those of Iry-Hor, Ka, Narmer, and Aha, and those of Djer to Qa'a are in the adjoining sector. The first three kings of the Second Dynasty were buried at Saqqara, and Peribsen and Khasekhemwy returned to Abydos.

hechos/mastaba-s3504-de-saqqara/resumen.texto: One of the largest mastabas of the First Dynasty, in the Saqqara necropolis, built shortly after 3000 BC in the reign of Djet and excavated by Walter Bryan Emery in 1953.

hechos/mastaba-s3035-de-saqqara/resumen.texto: Large mudbrick mastaba of the First Dynasty, about 57 x 26 m, with a niched façade imitating that of a palace, built around 3000 BC, very probably under Den. The name of the official Hemaka appears on many of its objects, so it is usually assumed to be his tomb; Firth excavated part of it in 1931 and Emery in 1936.

hechos/enterramientos-subsidiarios-de-dj.texto: Subsidiary burials in the tomb of Djer

The tomb of Djer at Umm el-Qaab has about 338 subsidiary burials. It is debated whether they indicate human sacrifice: the Palermo Stone records in year 4 of his reign a “following of Horus” and the burning of incense before a victim, which Helck attributed to the lady Penebui, and a Saqqara tag perhaps shows a human sacrifice.

hechos/barcos-funerarios-de-abidos/resum.texto: Fourteen boats of mudbrick and wood found next to the enclosure of Khasekhemwy, in a boat grave established before the end of the Second Dynasty and perhaps for Aha or Djer.

hechos/tumba-de-den-en-umm-el-qaab/titul.texto: Tomb of Den with a granite floor

hechos/tumba-de-den-en-umm-el-qaab/resum.texto: The tomb of Den, king of the First Dynasty, has a floor of red and black granite with a staircase, the earliest known use of granite as a building material in Egypt.

hechos/peribsen-adopta-a-set/titulo.texto: Peribsen adopts Seth as patron god

hechos/peribsen-adopta-a-set/resumen.texto: Peribsen put Seth and not Horus in his royal name, something that is not repeated in Egyptian history; Khasekhemwy, his presumed successor, included both.

hechos/gisr-el-mudir/resumen.texto: Large stone enclosure at Saqqara, one of the oldest known in Egypt, whose function is unknown. The pottery in the fill of its walls dates from the end of the Second Dynasty or the beginning of the Third, which leads some Egyptologists to think it was built at the end of the Second; its builder is not determined.

hechos/reunificacion-por-khasekhemwy/res.texto: After a division of the state toward the end of Nynetjer's reign, Khasekhemwy reunified Egypt around his year 13, according to Egyptologists. He combined Horus and Seth in his name.

hechos/shunet-el-zebib/resumen.texto: Large mudbrick enclosure at Abydos erected by Khasekhemwy, of the Second Dynasty, about 1.6 km from the royal tombs of Umm el-Qaab.

hechos/biblos-y-egipto-en-el-periodo-arc.texto: Byblos and Egypt in the Archaic period

Byblos wood appears in First Dynasty tombs, and the “ship of Byblos” is one of the oldest Egyptian words for a seagoing ship. At Byblos a fragment of a vessel bearing the name of Khasekhemwy was found, which may have arrived later; some authors maintain that in the Old and Middle Kingdoms it was almost an Egyptian colony.

hechos/piramide-estratificada-de-zawyet-.texto: Ruined stepped pyramid of the Third Dynasty whose owner is uncertain and may be Khaba. Its architecture is very similar to that of the pyramid of Sekhemkhet.

hechos/piramide-de-sekhemkhet/resumen.texto: Seven-stepped pyramid of Sekhemkhet, of the Third Dynasty, which was left unfinished.

hechos/relieves-reales-de-uadi-maghara/t.texto: Reliefs of Sanakht, Djoser, and Sekhemkhet at Wadi Maghara

hechos/relieves-reales-de-uadi-maghara/r.texto: At Wadi Maghara there are two reliefs of Sanakht, one of Djoser, and two almost identical ones of Sekhemkhet: expeditions of the Third Dynasty to the turquoise mines of Sinai. There are also tablets of Snefru, Khufu, Sahure, Nyuserre, Menkauhor, and Djedkare.

hechos/tumba-de-hesy-ra/resumen.texto: Tomb of a senior official of the Third Dynasty, famous for its paintings and its cedar wood panels.

hechos/piramide-de-seila/resumen.texto: One of seven small, very similar stepped pyramids, built far from Egypt's major centers, between the Faiyum and the Nile valley; Petrie discovered it in 1889-1890. Its builder may have been Snefru, the founder of the Fourth Dynasty.

hechos/piramide-sur-de-edfu/resumen.texto: Small stepped pyramid, of the same group of seven as that of Seila, about 5 km south of Edfu; Dreyer and Kaiser identified it as a pyramid in 1979. Its owner is disputed: Huni or his successor Snefru.

hechos/piramide-de-meidum/resumen.texto: The large pyramid of Meidum, the first smooth-sided pyramid in Egypt, which partly collapsed in antiquity. It is attributed to Snefru, and perhaps Huni began it.

hechos/piramide-acodada-de-snefru/resume.texto: The second of Snefru's three pyramids at Dahshur: its faces rise at 54 degrees and, from about 47 m up, at 43 degrees, which gives it its bent shape.

hechos/piramide-roja-de-snefru/resumen.texto: Snefru's pyramid at Dahshur, the largest in the necropolis and the first successful attempt at a smooth-sided pyramid.

hechos/campana-de-snefru-en-nubia-segun-.texto: Snefru's campaign in Nubia according to the Palermo Stone

Under Snefru the Palermo Stone records the capture in Nubia of 7,000 captives and 200,000 head of small livestock, the building of cedar ships and of the southern and northern walls called “Mansions of Snefru,” and the arrival of 40 ships loaded with conifer wood. The stone does not say where the campaign took place; Buhen is the nearest documented Egyptian site in Nubia.

hechos/fundicion-de-cobre-egipcia-en-buh.texto: In the Old Kingdom Buhen was an Egyptian colony in Nubia, notable for its copper smelting; in 1962 a metallurgical installation was found there.

hechos/explotacion-de-alabastro-en-hatnu.texto: The alabaster quarry and its workers' camp were used intermittently from at least the reign of Khufu.

hechos/puerto-de-uadi-al-jarf/resumen.texto: Artificial Red Sea harbor, the oldest known, with papyri from year 27 of Khufu and numerous storage jars. It lies opposite the Sinai fortress of Tell Ras Budran, across the Gulf of Suez.

hechos/transporte-de-caliza-de-tura-a-gi.texto: Transport of limestone from Tura to Giza

The Diary of Merer, from year 27 of Khufu, records the transport by boat of limestone blocks from Tura. The diary does not say where the blocks were used; they are linked to the casing of the Great Pyramid.

hechos/tumba-de-hetepheres-i/resumen.texto: The burial equipment of Queen Hetepheres I, wife of Snefru and mother of Khufu, was found in 1925 in shaft G 7000x, in the eastern cemetery at Giza next to the Great Pyramid. The sarcophagus was empty, and Reisner interpreted this as a reburial.

hechos/piramides-de-las-reinas-de-keops/.texto: Queens' pyramids of Khufu at Giza

Three subsidiary pyramids east of the Great Pyramid: G1-a, the northern one; G1-b, the central one, which Lehner and Stadelmann attribute to Meritites I and Hawass to an unknown queen of Khufu, mother of Djedefre; and G1-c, the southern one, of Henutsen, named by a New Kingdom stela.

hechos/barca-solar-de-keops/resumen.texto: A 43.4 m boat, sealed in a pit next to the Great Pyramid. It is one of the oldest, largest, and best-preserved vessels of antiquity.

hechos/piramide-de-djedefre/titulo.texto: Pyramid of Djedefre at Abu Rawash

hechos/piramide-de-djedefre/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Djedefre, the northernmost in Egypt, now almost in ruins; the report on its excavation was published in 2011.

hechos/piramide-de-kefren/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Khafre at Giza, the second largest after the Great Pyramid.

hechos/gran-esfinge-de-giza/resumen.texto: Colossal sculpture next to the complex of Khafre, to whom it is commonly attributed; its date and its builder have been debated.

hechos/estatua-de-kefren-entronizado/res.texto: Ka statue of Khafre in gneissic anorthosite, a hard dark stone brought by the Nile from Khafre's quarries west of Gebel el-Asr, about 1,000 km away. It was made for the valley temple of the king, next to the Great Sphinx, and is in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

hechos/piramide-de-micerino/resumen.texto: Third pyramid at Giza, the smallest of the three great ones.

hechos/piramide-g3-a-de-micerino/resumen.texto: One of three satellite pyramids of Menkaure's pyramid, south of it and the easternmost, 44 m on a side, perhaps built for a wife of Menkaure; Reisner believed it was for Khamerernebty II, which is far from certain. It may also have been a chapel where the king was mummified.

hechos/triadas-de-micerino/resumen.texto: Five greywacke high reliefs showing Menkaure standing between two other figures, found in the same place as a statue of him with his wife Khamerernebty II (the dyad of Menkaure).

hechos/tumba-de-meresankh-iii/resumen.texto: Tomb of the queen of Khafre at Giza, with a black granite sarcophagus given to her by her mother Hetepheres II; George Reisner discovered it in 1927.

hechos/busto-de-ankhhaf/resumen.texto: Painted limestone bust of Prince Ankhhaf, an Old Kingdom work considered the work of a master, now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

hechos/escriba-sentado-de-saqqara/resume.texto: Painted limestone statue of a seated scribe, with eyes inlaid with rock crystal, found in 1850 north of the sphinx avenue of the Serapeum of Saqqara and now in the Louvre. It is dated to the Fifth or Fourth Dynasty.

hechos/estatua-de-kaaper-sheikh-el-beled.texto: Wooden statue of very fine workmanship of the scribe and priest Kaaper, from the late Fourth or early Fifth Dynasty, known as Sheikh el-Beled.

hechos/mastabat-al-faraun/resumen.texto: Tomb of Shepseskaf, last king of the Fourth Dynasty, in South Saqqara. It is a mastaba and not a pyramid.

hechos/piramide-norte-inconclusa-de-zawy.texto: Unfinished northern pyramid of Zawyet el-Aryan
Large shaft of an unfinished Fourth Dynasty pyramid, which most Egyptologists attribute to a king with the Hellenized name Bikheris (from the Egyptian Baka); Helck and others doubt this attribution.

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-v/titulo.texto: Beginning of the Fifth Dynasty with Userkaf

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-v/resumen.texto: Userkaf founds the Fifth Dynasty. The Westcar Papyrus, a much later tale, presents Userkaf, Sahure, and Neferirkare as brothers, sons of Ra and Rededjet. Manetho calls the dynasty “kings of Elephantine,” perhaps through a misreading of Sakhebu, near Heliopolis.

hechos/piramide-de-userkaf/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Userkaf northeast of that of Djoser, now a cone of rubble that the locals call the “heap of stone.”

hechos/templo-solar-de-userkaf/resumen.texto: Temple of Userkaf's sun god Ra, between Abusir and Abu Gurab, with the ancient name “stronghold of Ra.”

hechos/templo-de-montu-en-el-tod/resumen.texto: The oldest object found at El-Tod is a granite column of Userkaf, which makes him the oldest king attested in the temple of Montu at that site, southwest of Luxor.

hechos/piramide-de-sahure/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Sahure, which begins the constructions at Abusir on ground previously used by Userkaf. Ludwig Borchardt excavated it in 1907-1908.

hechos/expedicion-de-sahure-a-punt/lugar.texto: Abusir (reliefs of the temple of Sahure)

hechos/expedicion-de-sahure-a-punt/resum.texto: Sahure sent the first documented expedition to the land of Punt, probably along the coast of Somalia according to Verner, from which they returned with myrrh, malachite, and electrum. Campaigns against Libyan chiefs and sea voyages to the Levant also date from his reign; Punt is not located with certainty, and the marked point is the temple with the reliefs.

hechos/piramide-de-neferirkare/resumen.texto: Pyramid of the third king of the Fifth Dynasty at Abusir, whose funerary temple produced part of the Abusir Papyri.

hechos/piramide-de-khentkaus-ii/titulo.texto: Pyramid of Khentkaus II at Abusir

hechos/piramide-de-khentkaus-ii/resumen.texto: Pyramid complex of Queen Khentkaus II, wife of Neferirkare and mother of two kings, at Abusir.

hechos/piramide-de-neferefre/resumen.texto: Unfinished pyramid of Neferefre, the third on the Abusir diagonal; Nyuserre hastily finished it in the form of a mastaba.

hechos/piramide-lepsius-xxiv/resumen.texto: Largely destroyed pyramid, east of that of Neferefre and south of that of Khentkaus II, probably built for a wife of Nyuserre.

hechos/piramide-doble-de-abusir/resumen.texto: Pair of adjoining monuments on the southeastern edge of Abusir, from the middle of the Fifth Dynasty, probably of Nyuserre, for two women of the extended royal family. Verner sees them as a type of tomb of its own, the “double pyramid,” and Magdolen as a simple double mastaba.

hechos/templo-solar-de-nyuserre/titulo.texto: Sun temple of Nyuserre Ini at Abu Gurab

hechos/templo-solar-de-nyuserre/resumen.texto: The largest surviving sun temple of the Old Kingdom (Shesepibre) and one of the best preserved in ancient Egypt.

hechos/piramide-de-nyuserre/resumen.texto: Pyramid of the sixth king of the Fifth Dynasty at Abusir.

hechos/complejo-funerario-de-ptahshepses.texto: Mastaba complex of Ptahshepses at Abusir
Mastaba of the vizier Ptahshepses, son-in-law of Nyuserre Ini, considered by many to be the largest and most unusual in architecture of the private tombs of the Old Kingdom.

hechos/tumba-de-khentkaus-i/titulo.texto: Stepped tomb of Khentkaus I at Giza

hechos/tumba-de-khentkaus-i/resumen.texto: Two-step tomb (LG100) of the queen mother Khentkaus I, formerly known as the fourth pyramid of Giza and built in two phases, with a core of quarry rock faced with Tura limestone. Its form leads some to think the owner ruled in her own right.

hechos/piramide-decapitada-de-saqqara/re.texto: Remains of a pyramid complex in northern Saqqara whose owner is unclear: Menkauhor of the Fifth Dynasty or Merikare of the Tenth is suspected. The substructure was investigated between 2005 and 2008 by a team led by Zahi Hawass.

hechos/piramide-de-djedkare-isesi/resume.texto: Pyramid of King Djedkare Isesi in South Saqqara.

hechos/piramide-de-unas-y-textos-de-las-.texto: Pyramid of Unas and the earliest Pyramid Texts
Pyramid of Unas at Saqqara, the first in whose inner chambers the Pyramid Texts were carved.

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-vi/titulo.texto: Beginning of the Sixth Dynasty with Teti

hechos/comienzo-de-la-dinastia-vi/resume.texto: Teti begins the Sixth Dynasty. Manetho says he was killed by his guards and does not mention Userkare, whom the Abydos King List gives; the harem conspiracy is from Weni's biography and took place under Pepi I. The Turin Canon's number of years for Teti is destroyed, and archaeology does not confirm that death.

hechos/piramide-de-teti/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Teti at Saqqara, with Pyramid Texts.

hechos/conjura-del-harem-contra-pepi-i/r.texto: Probably after his year 20, Pepi I faced a conspiracy hatched in the harem by one of his consorts, who perhaps wanted her son to be named heir. Weni, who investigated the case, recounts it in his autobiography.

hechos/alianza-de-pepi-i-con-la-familia-.texto: Alliance of Pepi I with the family of Khui of Abydos
