After the harem conspiracy, Pepi I strengthened his power by allying himself with Khui, nomarch of Abydos: he married two of his daughters, Ankhesenpepi I and II, and made his wife Nebet and his son Djau viziers. This may also have compensated for the weakening of royal power.

hechos/campanas-de-weni-contra-los-habit.texto: Campaigns of Weni against the peoples of the east

Under Pepi I, Weni led an army against the peoples of the east, according to his autobiography. The text does not locate the campaign precisely; the marked point, in Sinai, is only the nearest documented site.

hechos/piramide-de-pepi-i/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Pepi I in South Saqqara, with Pyramid Texts.

hechos/canal-de-merenre-en-la-primera-ca.texto: Canal of Merenre at the First Cataract
Merenre had a canal dug to ease navigation past the First Cataract toward Nubia, out of interest in the trade of the region.

hechos/exploraciones-de-harkhuf-en-nubia.texto: Harkhuf, a native of Elephantine, made four journeys to the land of Yam in Upper Nubia, three under Merenre and the fourth in year 2 of Pepi II; Yam is known mainly from this autobiography. He returned with exotic products, including a dwarf for the young king.

hechos/expedicion-de-sabni-a-nubia/resum.texto: Sabni, of Qubbet el-Hawa, traveled to Nubia to recover the body of his father Mekhu, who had died there on an earlier expedition.

hechos/piramide-de-merenre/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Merenre Nemtyemsaf I in South Saqqara, with Pyramid Texts.

hechos/reinado-de-pepi-ii/resumen.texto: Pepi II came to the throne as a child, and his reign, one of the longest attributed to a king (94 years according to Manetho), coincides with the growth of the power of the nomarchs and the decline of kingship. The documents of his time reach his year 62.

hechos/piramide-de-pepi-ii/resumen.texto: Pyramid of Pepi II in South Saqqara, with Pyramid Texts.

hechos/decretos-de-pepi-ii-en-coptos/tit.texto: Decrees of Pepi II at Coptos

hechos/decretos-de-pepi-ii-en-coptos/res.texto: Stelae from the temple of Min at Coptos preserve decrees of Pepi II about the temple and its personnel.

hechos/complejo-funerario-de-qar/titulo.texto: Funerary complex of the vizier Qar at Abusir

hechos/complejo-funerario-de-qar/resumen.texto: Tomb of the vizier Qar of the Sixth Dynasty, found in 1995 by a Czech expedition; it was enlarged when Qar passed from a minor office to that of vizier.

hechos/mastaba-de-mereruka/resumen.texto: Large mastaba of Teti's vizier, who held offices such as director of the king's works and chief of the readers.

hechos/tumba-de-ibi-en-deir-el-gabrawi/t.texto: Tomb of Ibi at Deir el-Gabrawi

hechos/tumba-de-ibi-en-deir-el-gabrawi/r.texto: Rock-cut tomb of Ibi, nomarch of Ta-wer, the eighth nome of Upper Egypt, and of Dyu-ef, the 12th nome, at the end of the Sixth Dynasty.

hechos/evento-climatico-de-2200-a-c/titu.texto: Climate event of 2200 BC (4.2 ka event)

hechos/evento-climatico-de-2200-a-c/resu.texto: An episode of aridification around 2200 BC, which probably lasted the whole of the 22nd century BC. Harvey Weiss and others propose it as the cause of the collapse of the Old Kingdom in Egypt and of the Akkadian Empire, with Tell Leilan as a key site; other specialists point out that several sites remained inhabited, attribute the decline to internal causes, and hold that it was not a global drought nor had a clear chronology.

hechos/piramide-de-qakare-ibi/resumen.texto: Small pyramid of King Ibi, of the Eighth Dynasty, in South Saqqara: the main evidence of his reign.

hechos/decretos-de-coptos-de-la-dinastia.texto: Coptos decrees of the Eighth Dynasty

Decrees g through r, of kings of the Eighth Dynasty, raise Shemay of Coptos to governor and vizier of Upper Egypt and benefit his son Idy; Decree r deals only with Idy's welfare, and Hayes reads it as a sign of the king's weakness.

hechos/piramide-de-khui/resumen.texto: Ruined pyramid in the royal necropolis of Dara, near Manfalut and the entrance to the Dakhla oasis, attributed to Khui, of the Eighth Dynasty or a nomarch who proclaimed himself king, with a funerary temple and a mudbrick enclosure.

hechos/inscripciones-de-tjauti-en-gebel-.texto: Inscriptions of Tjauti at Gebel Tjauti

Rock inscriptions of the official Tjauti, from the end of the Eighth Dynasty, found by the Theban Desert Road Survey; one seems to speak of the opening of a road and of struggles. Next to it is another that names a king Intef, whom the publication identifies with Intef I, and an attack by soldiers.

hechos/guerra-de-anjtifi-contra-tebas/re.texto: The autobiography of Anjtifi recounts his resistance to Thebes and his restoration of order in the nomes of Edfu and Hierakonpolis, as well as the suffering of the population.

hechos/hambruna-en-tiempos-de-anjtifi/ti.texto: Famine in Upper Egypt according to Anjtifi

hechos/hambruna-en-tiempos-de-anjtifi/re.texto: The tomb of Anjtifi describes the suffering of the people in his time and his distribution of food; it is the main source on the crisis of Upper Egypt.

hechos/guerra-entre-tebas-y-heracleopoli.texto: War between Thebes and Herakleopolis over Abydos

Intef II clashed with the kings of Herakleopolis Magna over the possession of Abydos, around 2100 BC. According to the Instruction for Merikare and the biography of Tefibi, the Herakleopolitans retook Tinis and plundered its necropolis.

hechos/piramide-de-merikare/resumen.texto: Pyramid that has not been identified, attested by inscriptions on funerary stelae and perhaps at Saqqara; it would be the tomb of the Herakleopolitan king Merikare, of the Tenth Dynasty. It is sometimes identified with the Decapitated Pyramid, although that one is more probably Menkauhor's.

hechos/expansion-tebana-en-la-baja-nubia.texto: A statue of Intef II in the shrine of Heqaib at Elephantine, and the expedition of Djemi from Gebelein to Wawat, suggest that his authority reached the First Cataract and perhaps part of Lower Nubia.

hechos/intef-iii-toma-asiut/resumen.texto: Intef III defended what his father had won, as the tomb of Nakhty at Abydos attests, and he conquered territories north of Abydos, especially Asyut, perhaps as far as the 17th nome.

hechos/tumba-de-tefibi-en-asiut/titulo.texto: Tomb III of Asyut, of Tefibi

hechos/tumba-de-tefibi-en-asiut/resumen.texto: Tomb of Tefibi, nomarch of Asyut in the Tenth Dynasty, with his biography inscribed.

hechos/apogeo-del-grupo-a-en-la-baja-nub.texto: Peak of the A-Group in Lower Nubia
The A-Group was the first powerful society of Nubia, between the First and Second Cataracts; it reached its peak around 3100 BC and fell about two centuries later.

hechos/origen-de-la-cultura-de-kerma/res.texto: The Kerma culture developed from c. 2500 BC in Upper Nubia and reached its peak between 1750 and 1500 BC.

hechos/cultura-del-grupo-c/resumen.texto: Archaeological culture of Lower Nubia, from c. 2400 to 1550 BC, which emerges toward the end of the Old Kingdom and has no main center: Aniba is only one site in the region, with its own cemeteries and those of the A-Group. George Reisner gave it its name.

lugares/umm-el-qaab/resumen.texto: Necropolis of Abydos, with the predynastic Tomb U-j and the tombs of the kings of the First and Second Dynasties. Its Arabic name means “mother of pots.”

lugares/hieracompolis/resumen.texto: Religious and political capital of Upper Egypt at the end of prehistory (c. 3200-3100 BC) and probably in the early dynastic period; the Painted Tomb dates from c. 3500-3200 BC. The Narmer Palette and the Scorpion Macehead were found there.

lugares/buto/resumen.texto: City of the northwestern Delta, today Tell el-Fara'in, the main cult center of the cobra goddess Wadjet. It gives its name, together with Maadi, to the predynastic Lower Egyptian culture.

lugares/nagada/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian town that gives its name to the Naqada culture. In its necropolis lies the great mastaba attributed to Neithhotep.

lugares/dahshur/resumen.texto: Royal necropolis south of Memphis, opened by Snefru with the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid. It also has Middle Kingdom pyramids.

lugares/meidum/resumen.texto: Site with a large pyramid, the first smooth-sided pyramid in Egypt, which partly collapsed in antiquity, perhaps begun by Huni, and several mudbrick mastabas.

lugares/abusir/resumen.texto: Pyramid complex of the Fifth Dynasty, with those of Sahure, Neferirkare, Neferefre, and Nyuserre, and mastabas of senior officials. The Abusir Papyri came from the funerary temples.

lugares/abu-gorab/resumen.texto: Place north of Abusir known for the sun temples of Userkaf and Nyuserre Ini, the latter one of the best preserved.

lugares/abu-rawash/resumen.texto: Site north of Giza, with the pyramid of Djedefre, the northernmost in Egypt, in ruins.

lugares/zawyet-el-aryan/resumen.texto: Necropolis with tomb Z 401, which has a seal of Iry-Hor, the Layer Pyramid of the Third Dynasty, tentatively attributed to Khaba, and an unfinished northern pyramid of the Fourth Dynasty. Most Egyptologists attribute the latter to a king known by the Hellenized name Bikheris, although Helck and others doubt it.

lugares/heracleopolis/resumen.texto: Capital of the 20th nome of Upper Egypt, near Beni Suef, and seat of the kings of the Ninth and Tenth Dynasties during the First Intermediate Period. The Palermo Stone already records a visit by Den, around the middle of the First Dynasty, to its sacred lake.

lugares/asiut/resumen.texto: Capital of the 13th nome of Upper Egypt, allied with the Herakleopolitan kings; its nomarch tombs, such as that of Tefibi, preserve biographies from the First Intermediate Period.

lugares/qubbet-el-hawa/resumen.texto: Necropolis of nobles and priests across from Aswan, in use from the Fourth Dynasty; it holds the tombs of Harkhuf and Sabni.

lugares/hatnub/resumen.texto: Alabaster quarry and seasonal workers' settlement in the eastern desert, used from at least the reign of Khufu.

lugares/wadi-maghara/resumen.texto: Site in southwestern Sinai with turquoise mines and pharaonic monuments from the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms. It has reliefs of Sanakht, Djoser, and Sekhemkhet.

lugares/wadi-al-jarf/resumen.texto: The oldest known artificial Red Sea harbor, with papyri from the time of Khufu, among them the Diary of Merer.

lugares/qustul/resumen.texto: Lower Nubian necropolis with A-Group tombs, opposite Ballana; it is now covered by Lake Nasser.

lugares/coptos/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian city, a center since the predynastic period and the starting point of the route to the Red Sea through Wadi Hammamat. Stelae with decrees of Pepi I and Pepi II survive, and others from the Eighth Dynasty.

lugares/el-tarif/resumen.texto: Theban necropolis where the large saff-style tombs of the kings Intef I, II, and III of the Eleventh Dynasty are located.

lugares/moalla/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian site with the tomb of Anjtifi, nomarch of the First Intermediate Period.

lugares/deir-el-gabrawi/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian necropolis of nomarchs with rock-cut tombs, such as that of Ibi, from the end of the Sixth Dynasty.

lugares/tura/resumen.texto: Main limestone quarry of ancient Egypt, between Cairo and Helwan.

lugares/gebelein/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian site, south of Thebes, with a predynastic necropolis famous for its natural mummies.

lugares/mastaba-de-ti/resumen.texto: Mastaba of an official of the Fifth Dynasty at Saqqara, with two serdabs and scenes of fields, fishing, hunting in the marshes, and boat building. According to Auenmüller, it is dated from Neferirkare to Nyuserre.

lugares/gebel-tjauti/resumen.texto: Rock formation in the Theban desert with inscriptions of the official Tjauti, from the end of the Eighth Dynasty, and another of a king Intef, identified with Intef I.

lugares/tinis/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian city whose necropolis is Abydos; later tradition makes it the cradle of the first kings. Mentuhotep II mentions it in the name of his year 14.

lugares/meir/resumen.texto: Necropolis of Upper Egyptian nomarchs with tombs from the end of the Old Kingdom.

lugares/edfu/resumen.texto: Upper Egyptian city, capital of the 2nd nome, whose tell preserves the development of a provincial town from the end of the Old Kingdom. It is one of the nomes in which Anjtifi was active.

lugares/dendera/resumen.texto: Capital of the 6th nome of Upper Egypt, whose governor was sometimes chief of all Upper Egypt, such as Idu I at the end of the Sixth Dynasty. The temple of Hathor is attributed to Pepi I.

lugares/el-tod/resumen.texto: Site of a temple of Montu southwest of Luxor, whose oldest object is a granite column of Userkaf, which makes him the oldest king attested there.

lugares/tarkhan/resumen.texto: Necropolis south of Cairo, with more than 2,000 tombs excavated by Petrie, mostly of Naqada IIIA2-IIIB, and mastabas of the First Dynasty. Sealings bearing the name of King Narmer were found there, as well as the Tarkhan Dress.

lugares/minshat-abu-omar/resumen.texto: Site in the eastern Delta with several protodynastic cemeteries: 420 tombs from the end of Naqada III to the beginning of the First Dynasty. Objects of Levantine origin show trade with the Levant already in Naqada III.

lugares/tell-el-farkha/resumen.texto: Settlement in the eastern Delta occupied from c. 3700 to c. 2600 BC, with the Lower Egyptian culture, early Naqada, and the protodynastic period. Three serekhs of Iry-Hor were found in tombs there.

lugares/kom-el-hisn/resumen.texto: Old Kingdom settlement in the western Delta, in the 3rd nome of Lower Egypt, which may be the ancient capital Imu. It has a necropolis and a temple of Sekhmet-Hathor.

lugares/beit-khallaf/resumen.texto: Village west of Girga, in Upper Egypt, with mudbrick mastabas of the Third Dynasty; in one of them, K1, a seal bearing the name of Djoser led Garstang to believe it was his tomb. The article refers to the present-day village.

lugares/el-hawawish/resumen.texto: Necropolis of Akhmim, in the 9th nome of Upper Egypt, with tombs of nomarchs of the Old Kingdom and the First Intermediate Period, on the hill of El Hawawish.

lugares/dakhla/resumen.texto: Oasis of the Western Desert whose first contacts with pharaonic power are dated to around 2550 BC. About 500 tablets were found in the governor's palace at Ain Asil (Balat).

lugares/abu-ballas/resumen.texto: Two sandstone hills in the Libyan Desert, covered with jars, which served as a depot on a route of the Western Desert, set up at the end of the Old Kingdom or the beginning of the First Intermediate Period. The site was occupied in the Neolithic, between c. 6700 and 3700 BC.

lugares/tell-ras-budran/resumen.texto: Circular fort of the Fourth Dynasty on the Sinai coast of the Gulf of Suez, near copper and turquoise mines, contemporary with the Wadi al-Jarf harbor, across from it. It is among the oldest forts with battlements and bastions.

lugares/aniba/resumen.texto: Village of Lower Nubia, about 230 km south of Aswan, now covered by Lake Nasser; the oldest remains date to around 3000 BC and belong to A-Group cemeteries. The region was one of the most fertile in Lower Nubia.

lugares/mendes/resumen.texto: City of the eastern Delta, capital of the 16th nome of Lower Egypt, attested at least since Naqada II; it has an Old Kingdom necropolis with more than 9,000 burials.

lugares/bubastis/resumen.texto: City of the Delta, capital of its nome and center of the cult of the goddess Bastet, whose settlement began at the end of the 4th millennium BC. Worship of Bastet is attested from the reign of Hotepsekhemwy, in the Second Dynasty.

lugares/tell-es-sakan/resumen.texto: Mound 5 km south of Gaza, founded as an administrative center for the Egyptian colonies of southwestern Canaan; it was occupied between c. 3300 and 3000 BC. When it was discovered in 1998, it was the oldest known Egyptian fortification and the only one outside the Nile valley.
